findings.quote:
/**
 * Extension for [ProxyHints.registerJdkProxy] providing a [KClass] based variant.
 *
 * @author Sebastien Deuze
 * @since 6.0.5
 */
fun ProxyHints.registerJdkProxy(vararg proxiedInterfaces: KClass<*>) =
	registerJdkProxy(*proxiedInterfaces.map { it.java }.toTypedArray())
findings.explanation: The extension maps each KClass one-for-one to its Java Class, converts the result to an array, and spreads it into the Java Class<?> vararg overload. Mapping preserves argument order and repetitions; an empty input produces an empty Class array. Its expression-body return is the Java method's return, which is the same ProxyHints receiver. The Kotlin test stubs that Class-vararg method to return the mock and verifies the exact String::class.java, Int::class.java call in that order. Because the result is ignored, the test does not independently assert fluent identity. More importantly, the mock bypasses validation and storage: String and primitive int are not interfaces, so those examples prove conversion and delegation only, not that real Class-based registration accepts them.

findings.quote:
/**
 * Extension for [JdkProxyHint.Builder.proxiedInterfaces] providing a [KClass] based variant.
 *
 * @author Sebastien Deuze
 * @since 6.0.5
 */
fun JdkProxyHint.Builder.proxiedInterfaces(vararg proxiedInterfaces: KClass<*>) =
	proxiedInterfaces(*proxiedInterfaces.map { it.java }.toTypedArray())
findings.explanation: This performs the same stable, duplicate-preserving KClass-to-Class conversion and hands off to Builder.proxiedInterfaces(Class<?>...). Its inferred return is that Java method's return—the same builder—so chaining remains possible. The related MockK test stubs the Class-vararg method to return the builder and verifies the exact String/Int Java-Class arguments in order. It does not exercise the real builder, validation, hint construction, or registration, and it ignores the returned value; therefore its example types establish only the handoff, not valid proxy-interface inputs.

The TypeReference overload wraps its unchanged array in a consumer; the Class<?> overload does the same with Builder.proxiedInterfaces(Class<?>...). Both therefore converge on the consumer entry point. Every registration allocates a fresh, initially empty builder, invokes the callback, builds a hint, inserts that whole hint, and only then returns the same ProxyHints. If the callback, Class validation, or build throws, insertion is never reached: existing entries remain, and no empty or partially configured hint is stored. Any builder state accumulated before the failure remains only in that local, unregistered builder under the stated consumer scope.

Both overloads append to a LinkedList and return the same builder; they do not replace, sort, or deduplicate prior entries. Repeated calls concatenate their inputs, repeated arguments remain repeated, and empty arrays are no-ops. The separately inspected Class helper first scans the entire supplied array and collects every Class that is not an interface or is sealed. If that list is nonempty, it throws before converting or appending anything from that call. Otherwise TypeReference.listOf maps each Class in order through TypeReference.of(Class), producing reflection-backed references. The TypeReference overload instead appends references directly and performs no interface or sealed check. That route can represent unresolved/name-only types and has no Class metadata on which to perform those checks; the Java tests accordingly demonstrate that name-backed references are accepted while concrete and sealed Class inputs are rejected.

Each JdkProxyHint.of overload creates a fresh builder, performs the corresponding initial addition, and returns the builder—it neither builds nor registers a hint. Building copies the interface list with List.copyOf and snapshots both metadata fields into final hint fields. The exposed list is therefore unmodifiable, and later additions or metadata changes on the builder cannot alter an already built hint. Empty builders build successfully with an empty immutable list. For the requested contract-violating case, Arrays.asList and LinkedList accept a null element in an otherwise non-null TypeReference array, so the TypeReference builder call—and JdkProxyHint.of(TypeReference...) itself—can return normally with latent null state. List.copyOf rejects that null with NullPointerException during build. Through ProxyHints registration, this occurs before Set insertion, leaving the registry unchanged.

A new builder defaults to no reachable type (null) and Java serialization disabled (false). The separately inspected onReachableType(TypeReference) and withJavaSerialization(boolean) methods assign their fields and return the same builder; repeated calls overwrite, so the last value wins, including setting serialization back to false. Construction snapshots those values, exposed by getReachableType() and hasJavaSerialization(). Equality requires the ordered interface list, reachable type, and serialization flag all to match. Notably, hashCode hashes only the interface list: reachable type and serialization affect equality but not the hash. Thus metadata variants with identical interfaces are unequal yet intentionally collide, which a Set resolves through equality.

TypeReference.of(Class) creates a ReflectionTypeReference, while TypeReference.of(String) creates a SimpleTypeReference; both built-in implementations inherit this equality and hashing. Consequently, a Class-backed reference and a well-formed name-backed reference for the same canonical type compare equal and hash equally despite different backing. TypeReference.listOf(Class<?>...) maps in encounter order through the Class factory. This canonical-name identity is why mixed Class/name hints can deduplicate, while the name-based registration route can still avoid loading or introspecting a Class.

The registry inserts completed JdkProxyHint values into a LinkedHashSet and streams that set directly. Equal whole hints are suppressed, and iteration follows first-successful-insertion order; registering an equal hint later neither adds nor moves it. Class-backed and name-backed references for the same canonical types therefore deduplicate when the complete ordered lists and metadata match, as the Java tests demonstrate. List equality is order- and multiplicity-sensitive: reordering interfaces or introducing/removing/repositioning repetitions creates a distinct hint. Changing reachable type or the serialization flag also creates a distinct hint despite the metadata-independent hashCode. Repeated identical empty hints deduplicate, while empty hints with different metadata do not. Deduplication applies only to complete hints: registering [A] and later [A, B] stores two hints in that order; it never merges interface lists.
